questions.q: What is the key difference between a linter and a static analyzer, per this lesson?
options: They are the same tool with different names
A linter checks style/convention; a static analyzer reasons about control/data flow to flag vulnerability patterns
A linter only works on Hardhat projects, a static analyzer only on Foundry
A static analyzer executes the code; a linter never reads the code at all
questions.explain: A linter cares about how code is written (formatting, naming); a static analyzer reasons about what the code does, without executing it, to flag risky patterns.

questions.q: What does `forge fmt --check` do in a CI pipeline?
options: Automatically fixes and commits formatting issues
Fails the build on unformatted code without rewriting any files
Runs Slither on the formatted code
Deploys the contract if formatting passes
questions.explain: Like Lesson 8 covered, --check reports failures without modifying files, keeping the tested branch exactly what gets checked.

questions.q: What are the two rule categories in Solhint, Solidity's standard linter?
options: Gas rules and deployment rules
Security rules (e.g. flagging block.timestamp reliance) and Style Guide rules (naming, explicit visibility)
Frontend rules and backend rules
Testnet rules and mainnet rules
questions.explain: Solhint splits its rule set into Security rules and Style Guide rules — the security rules are a shallow preview of what deeper static analysis tools check.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend ordering a lint job before a full test job in a multi-job CI pipeline, using `needs: lint`?
options: GitHub Actions requires alphabetical job ordering
Linting is cheap and fast — fail fast on trivial mistakes before spending CI minutes on a longer test or scan job
Tests can only run after formatting is applied, or they won't compile
needs: lint is required syntax for all GitHub Actions workflows
questions.explain: Ordering cheap, fast checks first (via `needs:`) means the pipeline fails fast on trivial issues instead of burning CI minutes on expensive jobs first.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why are Solhint's security-category rules not a substitute for Lesson 10's tools (Slither, Mythril)?
options: Because Solhint only works on JavaScript, not Solidity
Because Solhint's security rules are a cheap, shallow preview — they don't trace actual control and data flow the way dedicated static analyzers do
Because Solhint has been deprecated
Because Solhint can only run locally, never in CI
questions.explain: The lesson frames Solhint's security rules as catching the obvious, cheaply, while deeper tools like Slither and Mythril reason about control/data flow in far more depth.
